narrative.what_i_did:
The operator opened with a specific security directive: when creating a wallet make sure no user can just click through and do a regular password manager mistake, and double-warn before letting the passphrase get set. I grounded against the two surfaces that capture a new passphrase — PassphrasePrompt.tsx for the Classic first-login path and FreshOnboarding.tsx's PassphraseStep for the Fresh onboarding state machine — and confirmed both currently flow straight from form-submit into wallet creation (or in Fresh's case, into the recovery primer that the wallet creation depends on) with only field-match plus eight-character minimum validation between the typed passphrase and the actual encryption key going live. CLAUDE_ROOT.md rule one — the user's keys never leave the wallet unencrypted — makes a clickthrough mistake terminal because the cloud-sync blob is undecryptable without the passphrase and there is no email reset path.

I surfaced a chip-form to pick the shape of the double-warn — two sequential modals, a single modal with two checkboxes, or an inline panel below the form. The operator chose Other with a free-text answer that reframed the directive: the design should emphasize that the passphrase is something PERSONAL the user picks, something they would remember on their own, and a password manager is fine for BACKUP but the passphrase needs to live in their head first. The transcription artifact 'past phrase' read as 'passphrase' — the operator was emphasizing 'passphrase, not password.' The double-warn became two distinct acknowledgments: first a personal-and-memorable check protecting against the password-manager-autogenerated-random-string failure mode, second the irrecoverable-consequence statement.

I cut a new shared component at src/features/wallet-core/PassphraseCommitWarnings.tsx that owns the two-step warning sequence with variant-specific styling for Classic and Fresh. The component takes a variant prop plus onConfirm and onBack callbacks plus optional busy and error props, and renders the appropriate warning step based on internal state. Step one headline reads 'Could you remember this without your password manager?' with body copy emphasizing that the passphrase needs to be personal — a line from a song, a memory in words, a phrase that means something only to the user — and that password manager backup is smart but the passphrase needs to live in the user's head first. Step two headline reads 'Last check: this is the only way back in.' with body copy stating the no-reset / no-support / no-email-recovery truth. Two button rows on each step let the operator advance or back out.

PassphrasePrompt.tsx now manages a warningsOpen state. The form-submit handler validates field-match plus minimum length and then opens the warnings rather than calling onSubmit directly. The warnings component's onConfirm callback is what actually triggers wallet creation, and a failure path sets the error and closes the warnings so the user can adjust. The form headline changed from 'Choose a passphrase' to 'Pick a passphrase only you would know' and the body copy now leads with the personal-memorable framing plus the password-manager-backup note. The form-submit button label changed from 'Create my wallet' to 'Continue' because clicking it no longer creates a wallet — it opens the gate.

FreshOnboarding.tsx grew a new 'passphrase-warn' step between 'passphrase' and 'recovery' in the state-machine union. The submitPassphrase handler now sets the step to 'passphrase-warn' rather than 'recovery' on successful field validation. The new step renders PassphraseCommitWarnings with variant fresh, an onConfirm that advances to 'recovery', and an onBack that returns to the passphrase form. RecoveryStep's onBack was updated to land back on 'passphrase-warn' so the back-button chain stays coherent. The PassphraseStep's headline changed from 'Pick a passphrase.' to 'Pick a passphrase only you would know.' and the body copy gained the personal-memorable plus password-manager-backup framing matching the Classic surface.

The WalletProvider bundle chunk crossed its 9.5KB gz budget by ~70 bytes after the PassphraseCommitWarnings import landed via PassphrasePrompt's eager import edge. I audited the growth, confirmed it was intentional (the gate IS the operator-asked-for feature and runs on the first-login critical path where a React.lazy Suspense flash would land at the exact moment the warning needs to be unambiguous), and bumped the budget to 10KB with a comment explaining the bump in scripts/bundle-budget.mjs following the precedent set by the previous five bump comments in the same block. The wallet-core manifest gained PassphraseCommitWarnings.tsx in touches and a leading sentence in notes explaining the 2026-05-27 double-warn gate. All four gates green throughout the cut — typecheck silent, lint silent, 335 of 335 tests passing in 9.81s, build clean with the WalletProvider bundle at 9.58KB gz under the new 10KB budget and HomeScreen still at 22.17KB gz under its 22.5KB budget.

narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
Two honest observations. First, the warnings component renders inline rather than as a modal overlay. Both Classic and Fresh swap the form for the warnings on the same surface — the user does not see the form behind a dimmed backdrop, the form is just gone for the moment of acknowledgment. This was a deliberate choice for consistency with how PassphrasePrompt and FreshOnboarding's existing steps render (they are all full-surface replacements, not stacked modals), but a reviewer could reasonably argue that a stacked modal makes the gate feel more weighty and explicit. If field-testing surfaces a sense that the gate is too easy to bypass mentally because the form just got replaced by another button page, switching to a modal-overlay variant is a one-component swap.

Second, the personal-memorable warning's affirmative button reads 'Yes — this is personal and I will remember it.' The operator's intent is to make the user PAUSE and actually answer the question. A passive reader could click the affirmative button reflexively without engaging with the question. A more aggressive variant would force a typed acknowledgment — for instance a checkbox that says 'Yes, I would remember this passphrase even without a password manager' that has to be checked before the button enables. I chose the lighter button-only variant to keep the friction proportional and avoid feeling like a TOS click-wrap, but if the operator wants harder gating the checkbox-required pattern is a clean addition.

Nothing else surfaced beyond the declared scope this session.
narrative.bigger_picture:
The bigger-picture teaching this session is what it means to put a security gate at the exact moment of consequence. The passphrase is the encryption key per CLAUDE_ROOT.md rule one — there is no email reset, no support team that can decrypt the cloud blob, no recovery path that does not require the passphrase. Every other line of the wallet codebase respects that invariant: the Wallet object holds keys, the storage layer holds ciphertext, the auth layer holds session tokens, and none of them can reconstitute the passphrase if it is lost. But the single moment where that invariant becomes the user's lived reality is the first-login passphrase capture — type a passphrase, click submit, and from that moment forward your wallet's entire sovereign-identity stack is encrypted under those bytes. If a password manager autofilled a random string and you clicked through without saving it, you are already dead and you do not know it yet. The gate this session shipped is the moment the user finds out before the action lands. Two distinct acknowledgments, two distinct moments of pause, because one is too easy to click through and three would feel like a TOS click-wrap.

The second teaching is what 'personal and memorable' means as a security property rather than a usability nicety. The Classic password-manager doctrine for the last twenty years has been 'generate a long random string per site and let the manager remember it for you.' That doctrine optimizes for breach-resistance against credential-stuffing attacks at remote services where the password is transmitted to a server that can be compromised. For a sovereign-identity wallet, the password never leaves the device, it is the encryption key for the keys themselves, and the threat model is not 'someone steals your password' but 'you lose your password and no one can help you.' Personal-and-memorable is the threat-model-appropriate posture. The user should pick something they would actually remember without their password manager, because the consequence of forgetting is total. Password managers can ALSO hold the passphrase as backup — the gate does not prohibit them — but the gate makes it impossible to commit a passphrase that the user has not actively committed to remembering. The operator's reframing of the directive landed exactly on this distinction.

The broader thesis-level connection is the same Layer 1 framing every session keeps reinforcing. Tapit Wallet is a sovereign-identity wallet, and 'sovereign' means 'no one else can recover for you.' Every other place in the codebase keeps the user as the sole holder of the master secret — never logged, never an env var, never transmitted unencrypted. The first-login flow is the moment the user accepts that sovereignty. The double-warn gate this session shipped is not a usability annoyance, it is the user being correctly informed of what they are about to commit to. The wallet's whole architectural integrity assumes the user understood and meant what they typed; this gate is what makes that assumption defensible. Operators of competing wallet products handle this badly — they show a single 'I understand' button and call it consent — and operators have been hurt by that. This gate is the operator's care for future operators landing on the same surface.

questions_asked.question: Which double-warn shape should both Classic + Fresh wallet creation gate on?
questions_asked.operator_answered: Other — free-text response reframing the directive: the passphrase should be something personal the user would remember on their own; password managers are fine as backup but the passphrase needs to live in the user's head first.
questions_asked.carpenters_read: The operator did not pick from the offered shapes; instead they reframed what the double-warn should be ABOUT rather than just how it should be SHAPED. The two acknowledgments now have different content — warning one asks whether the passphrase is personal-and-memorable (protection against the password-manager-autogenerated-random-string clickthrough mistake), warning two states the irrecoverable consequence. The shape I picked from the original options was two sequential acknowledgments because that most directly satisfies 'double warn' as two distinct moments of pause, but the content of those acknowledgments came from the operator's reframing not from my chip-form.

operator_directives: When creating a wallet make sure no user can just click through and do a regular password manager mistake. Double warn before letting passphrase get set.

I would like to have it where you do something that's personal to you not just a password. You can use the password manager, but it needs to also be something that's personal to you. A passphrase — emphasize a passphrase not a password, but it can be used in a password manager, but you would remember it first.

feedback_to_appcommander: The chip-form Other path landed cleanly this session. I offered three bounded shapes for the double-warn, the operator picked Other and used the free-text to reframe what the warning should be ABOUT rather than just its shape. The PFOR-019 doctrine works in both directions: when the carpenter has bounded shape choices the chip-form gates them, and when the operator wants to reframe the question itself, Other carries that signal cleanly. The reframing was richer than any of my three chips because the operator brought domain insight (the password-manager-autofill failure mode I had not named explicitly) that I could then translate into copy. One suggestion: consider naming this two-way pattern (chip-form-for-bounded-shape, Other-for-reframing) explicitly in the doctrine so future carpenters reach for chip-forms more readily even when they expect a reframe — the chip-form bounds my own assumptions and surfaces them for operator inspection, which is the bigger benefit than picking one of my pre-named shapes.
